FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
# Static site: the page, its modules and the guides. Tests stay out of the image.
COPY index.html calc.mjs usage.mjs robots.txt sitemap.xml marginal-roas-vs-average-roas.html /usr/share/nginx/html/
RUN printf 'types { text/javascript mjs; }\n' > /etc/nginx/conf.d/mjs.conf
EXPOSE 80
HEALTHCHECK CMD wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1/ >/dev/null || exit 1

README.md.text:
# Ad Spend Saturation Optimizer

A free browser tool for online sellers and marketers who run several ad channels:
**drop in weekly (or daily) spend and revenue per channel and see where the next dollar still pays and where it
does not.** It fits a diminishing-returns curve to each channel's own history, reads the marginal return at today's
spend, finds the split of the same total budget that earns most, and back-tests itself on your last weeks. Nothing
is uploaded.

**Live tool:** https://duncan-haywood.github.io/monorepo-projects/ad-spend-saturation-optimizer/

After using this, you can now **move budget from saturated channels to ones with headroom, see whether a channel's
next dollar loses money at your margin, and know how much to trust the advice before you act on it**.

## Input

One row per date and channel: a date, a channel (or source, platform, campaign), the spend, and the revenue you
credit to that channel. Columns are found by header name; a file without a channel column is treated as one channel.
Daily rows are summed into Monday weeks. Amounts in one currency.

## In a terminal

`node cli.mjs spend.csv` runs the same analysis from a file or `-` (stdin), with no dependencies and no network: `--margin 45`, `--skip "2025-11-24..2025-12-07"`, `--budget 12000` (best split of another weekly total), `--csv`, `--json`, `--example`, `--snapshot-out jan.json` (save the answers only, no rows) and `--since jan.json` (next month: how much of the suggested move was made and how each channel's marginal return changed). The web page has the same Save snapshot / Compare buttons. Tests in `cli.test.mjs`.

## Model

- Per channel, two response curves are fitted by least squares (Nelder-Mead in log space, multiple starts):
  saturating exponential `a (1 - exp(-s/k))` and S-shaped Hill `a s^h / (k^h + s^h)` with `h` in [0.5, 3]. The Hill
  curve is chosen only when it beats the exponential by more than 2 on small-sample AIC.
- Carry-over (adstock): for channels with 12+ weeks, a geometric carry-over rate of 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 or 0.8 is
  tried (`e = (1 - r) spend + r e_previous`, so steady spend is unchanged) and kept only if it beats no carry-over
  by more than 2 on small-sample AIC. The curve is then fitted on the carried spend and read at steady weekly spend;
  weeks missing from the file count as zero spend. The back-test re-picks the rate on its training weeks only.
- Promotion weeks: list date ranges in "Weeks to leave out" (`2025-11-24..2025-12-07; 2025-12-26`). Those weeks stay in the carry-over but are left out of the curve fit, the resamples, the "today's spend" average and the back-test score, so one Black Friday does not pull a channel's ceiling up (`parseSkipWeeks`, `kept` in `calc.mjs`). A channel left with under 8 weeks says so.
- Marginal return at today's spend (mean of the last 8 weeks) is the curve's slope there.
- Allocation: exact dynamic programme over the channels on a 400-step budget grid, so S-shaped curves are handled
  properly. Each channel is limited to 0.25x to 2x its current spend and never beyond 1.25x its highest week.
- Uncertainty: 100 seeded resamples of the channel's own weeks give a 10th to 90th percentile range on marginal
  return and on the gain from the recommended split.
- Budget what-if: `budgetPlan` / `budgetLadder` read the best split of a different weekly total (-30% to +50%, or one you type) off the same frontier, with revenue, the marginal return of the last dollar, contribution, and the gain over cutting or raising every channel pro rata.
- Profit view: contribution = margin x revenue - spend; the tool reports where it peaks along the fitted frontier.
- Back-test: refit on the weeks before the last 4 to 12, predict revenue in those weeks from the spend that really
  happened, compare with a flat-ROAS line.
- Checked in unit tests by parameter recovery on simulated data with known curves, an analytic equal-marginal-return
  optimum, a brute-force check on S-shaped curves, and a check that the recommended split beats the current one
  under the true curves.

Not modelled: carry-over longer or shaped differently from a single geometric rate, seasonality and price changes (promotions only if you list the weeks), overlap or halo
between channels, attribution error (revenue is whatever the file credits to each channel, often platform-reported
and overstated), incrementality, and any channel with under 8 weeks or nearly constant spend (left where it is).
The resample range covers noise in the fit, not a wrong curve shape. Unverified against a published marketing
dataset.

## Run

Open `index.html` through any static server. Tests: `node --test`.

## Host your own copy

Your data stays in the browser, but you can serve the page from an address you control. It is a static site: the
server only hands out files and never sees what you load.

- **Docker:** `docker compose up -d`, then open <http://localhost:8080> (`Dockerfile` is nginx plus the page's files).
- **Fly.io:** `fly launch --copy-config --no-deploy --dockerfile Dockerfile`, then `fly deploy` (`fly.toml`).
- **Render:** deploy from your fork with `render.yaml` (static site, no paid plan needed).
- Nothing runs on the author's accounts. The Docker image has not been built in the session that added these files,
  so build it once and open the page before relying on it. Tests: `node --test deploy.test.mjs`.

## Disclaimer

**No warranty.** This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or
implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional.
**You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it**, and for meeting
any obligation it helps you prepare for. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no
liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Independent of ad platforms and analytics vendors; none is named or ranked.

**Privacy.** Nothing is uploaded. Anonymous feature counts (`analysis_run`, `example_loaded`, `file_loaded`,
`report_downloaded`) are kept only in local storage, can be switched off on the page, and honour Do Not Track.

**Best-effort hosting, no SLA.** These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or
taken offline without notice. Do not use this as a system of record.

Free and open source (MIT, see `LICENSE`). Optional support:
[GitHub Sponsors](https://github.com/sponsors/Duncan-Haywood).

index.html.text:
AD SPEND SATURATION OPTIMIZER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Where does the next ad dollar still pay?

Drop in weekly spend and revenue by channel. The tool fits a diminishing-returns curve to each channel's own history, shows the marginal return at today's spend (what the next dollar earns, not the average), finds the split of the same budget that earns most, and back-tests itself on your last weeks so you can see how far to trust it.

Your numbers never leave this browser tab. Statistical fit of data you supply, not advice. Not legal, tax, or financial advice.

Your spend and revenue

Margin sets the break-even: a channel needs a marginal return of 100 divided by your margin, so 1.67 per dollar at 60%. A promotion week (Black Friday, a sale) sells more than its spend explains and tilts the curve, so list those dates as ranges and the fit ignores them while the carry-over still counts their spend. Daily rows are added up into Monday weeks. Use one currency, and the revenue you credit to each channel.

Upload or paste your data, then click Fit the curves.

Result

Channels: today versus the recommended split

ChannelWeekly spend nowAverage ROASMarginal ROAS nowRange (10th-90th)Of ceilingRecommended spendChange

What if you spend more or less in total?

Each row is the best split of that weekly total on the fitted curves, against spreading the same total in proportion to today's spend. Marginal ROAS is what the last dollar of that total earns; contribution is margin times revenue minus spend. Totals the per-channel limits cannot reach are left out.

Weekly totalChangeRevenue (best split)Gain over pro rataMarginal ROASContribution

Fitted curves

Dots: your weeksLine: fitted curveRing: spend nowDiamond: recommended spend

Back-test: predicted vs actual revenue in your last weeks

ChannelPredicted (curve)Predicted (flat ROAS)ActualTypical weekly error, curveFlat ROAS

Fitted models

How it is calculated

Curves: each channel's weekly points (spend, revenue) are fitted by least squares with two shapes: a saturating exponential, a(1 - e^(-s/k)), and an S-shaped Hill curve, a s^h / (k^h + s^h), where the first dollars do less than the later ones. The S-shape is used only when it improves small-sample AIC by more than 2. Marginal return is the slope of the curve at the average of the last eight weeks' spend. Best split: an exact dynamic programme over a 400-step grid of the same total, so S-shaped curves are handled correctly; each channel stays between 0.25x and 2x its current spend and under 1.25x its highest week. Ranges: 100 seeded resamples of your own weeks. Profit view: margin times fitted revenue minus spend, along the fitted frontier.

Not modelled: carry-over beyond one decay rate per channel (a single geometric rate is fitted when it clearly helps), seasonality, promotions and price changes, overlap or halo between channels, attribution error (revenue is whatever your file credits to a channel, often platform-reported and overstated), incrementality, and any channel with under eight weeks or almost constant spend, which is left where it is. The resampled ranges cover noise in the fit, not a wrong curve shape. Unverified: checked against simulated data with known curves, an analytic optimum and a brute-force search in unit tests, not against a published marketing dataset.

Common questions

What is marginal ROAS and why does it matter more than average ROAS?

Average ROAS is total revenue divided by total spend. Marginal ROAS is what the next dollar earns. Because ad channels saturate, the marginal figure is always lower than the average and is the one that tells you where to put more money. A channel with a 3.0 average ROAS can have a marginal ROAS under 1.0 if it is already spending near its ceiling.

How does the tool find the best split of my budget?

For each channel it fits a diminishing-returns curve to your own weekly spend and revenue, then searches every split of the same total budget with an exact dynamic programme and keeps the one with the highest total fitted revenue. Each channel is limited to between a quarter and double its current spend, and never beyond 1.25 times its highest week, so the advice stays near spend you have actually tried.

What data do I need?

One row per date and channel with the date, the channel name, the spend and the revenue credited to that channel. Daily or weekly rows both work; daily rows are added up into weeks. Each channel needs at least eight weeks, and spend has to have varied. A channel whose spend never changed cannot show what happens when it does.

How accurate is it?

The tool tests itself. It refits on your data up to some weeks before the end, predicts revenue in the final weeks from the spend that really happened, and compares that with a flat ROAS line. If the curve does not beat the flat line, or the error is large, something other than spend, such as seasonality or promotions, is driving your revenue and the split should be tried on a small share of budget first. The resampled ranges show noise in the fit, not whether the curve shape is right.

What is it not good at?

It models carry-over from one week to the next as a single decay rate, and ignores seasonality, promotions, price changes, overlap between channels and brand effects. It uses whatever revenue your file credits to each channel, which is often platform-reported and overstated and is not proof that the ad caused the sale. It cannot see what happens at spend levels you have never run.

What does the profit view mean?

You enter your gross margin. Contribution is margin times fitted revenue minus ad spend. The tool reports the weekly total where that peaks along the fitted curves. It ignores everything except attributed revenue and ad spend, and the peak is usually flat, so treat it as a range to test rather than a target.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The file is read and analyzed in this browser tab. Nothing is sent to a server, there are no accounts or cookies, and the tool never stores your spend or revenue. A snapshot you save holds only the answers (spend, marginal return and recommendation per channel), in a file you keep.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified analyst. Results are statistical fits of the numbers you supply; they do not guarantee what a channel will return at a different spend. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for any budget decision you make.

Independent. Not affiliated with any ad platform, analytics vendor or agency, and none is named or ranked here.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you enter, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere.

Everything runs in your browser. Your spend and revenue are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (analysis_run, example_loaded, file_loaded, report_downloaded, snapshot_compared) are counted only in local storage on your device, never with any of your data, and are switched off by Do Not Track.

marginal-roas-vs-average-roas.html.text:
← Ad spend saturation optimizer

Marginal ROAS vs average ROAS: why a 1.95 ROAS channel can lose money

Average ROAS is revenue divided by spend over everything the channel has done. Marginal ROAS is what the next dollar returns at today's spend. Ad channels saturate, so the first dollars earn the most and the last earn the least. Every dashboard shows the average; budget decisions are made on the margin.

Open the free optimizer

The experiment

The tool's built-in invented example: four channels, 78 weeks of spend and revenue, a 60% margin, so a dollar of spend needs about $1.67 of revenue to break even. Each channel's curve was fitted to its own weeks; the marginal figure is the curve's slope at the last eight weeks' average spend, with a 10th to 90th percentile range from 100 resamples.

ChannelWeekly spendAverage ROASMarginal ROAS (range)Suggested weekly spend
Google Search$5,1073.142.60 (2.57–2.65)$8,658
Meta Prospecting$11,4292.032.03 (1.97–2.09)$13,653
TikTok$4,7881.950.97 (0.93–1.03)$3,063
Influencer$5,3161.351.11 (1.03–1.18)$1,265

What it shows

TikTok's average ROAS of 1.95 clears the 1.67 break-even line, so a dashboard calls it healthy. Its marginal ROAS of 0.97 is below the line, and below 1.00: the next dollar returns less than a dollar of revenue. Google Search is the opposite, with a marginal return of 2.60 and room to take more. Moving the same total budget along those slopes lifts fitted revenue by about $4,323 a week (about 7%), and the gain is positive in all 100 resamples. Fitted on the earlier weeks, the curve predicted the final 12 weeks to within about 5% a week, against about 13% for a flat-ROAS line.

This is one invented account whose curves were known in advance, so it shows the method works when its assumptions hold, not that your account looks like this. Real data carries seasonality, promotions, carry-over between weeks and overstated platform attribution, none of which the tool models.

Find the margin in your own channels

How to estimate it by hand

1. Look for weeks when spend changed

Marginal return can only be learned from variation. If a channel spent the same amount every week, no method can tell you the slope.

2. Compare high-spend and low-spend weeks

Divide the extra revenue in your heaviest weeks by the extra spend, relative to your lightest. That ratio is a crude marginal ROAS, and it is usually well below the average.

3. Set the break-even line

One divided by your margin. Anything under it on the margin is spend that does not pay for itself on attributed revenue.

4. Move gradually and test

Shift part of the budget, wait a few weeks, and check that revenue moved the way the curve said.

Questions

What is marginal ROAS?

Marginal ROAS is the extra revenue you get from the next dollar of ad spend in a channel at your current spend level. Average ROAS is total revenue divided by total spend. With diminishing returns the marginal figure is lower than the average.

What marginal ROAS do I need to break even?

One divided by your margin. At a 60% margin you need 1.67 revenue per extra dollar; at 40% you need 2.50. Use the margin on the product sold, before ad spend, and treat the figure as approximate because platform-reported revenue is often overstated.

Can I work out marginal ROAS from my own ad data?

Yes, if spend varied from week to week. Fit a diminishing-returns curve to weekly spend and revenue per channel and read its slope at today's spend. The free tool does this in your browser and shows a range and a back-test so you can judge how far to trust it.

No warranty. Free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. This page is general information, not legal, tax or financial advice, and it does not tell you how to spend your advertising budget. The example is invented and the numbers come from running this tool's own engine on it. Not affiliated with any ad platform.

Everything the optimizer does runs in your browser; your spend file is never uploaded. Free and open source: support is entirely optional. Related: customer lifetime value predictor, SaaS CAC payback calculator.
